Row: 2 Col: 1 Val: 8

theory: When should you use a sparse matrix representation?
When the majority of elements in the matrix are zero (typically sparsity > 60-70%).
What is the time complexity of accessing an element in a triplet-based sparse matrix?
$O(K)$ where $K$ is the number of non-zero elements, because you must scan the list.
How do you transpose a sparse matrix stored as triplets?
Swap the row and column values for every element and sort the resulting list primarily by the new column (old row) indices.
coding: Add two sparse matrices represented as triplets
Use a two-pointer merge approach similar to merging two sorted lists based on `(row, col)` coordinates.
Fast transpose of a sparse matrix
Use frequency arrays and starting position arrays to achieve $O(non\_zeros + cols)$ transpose time without sorting.

dsa.recursion.explain:
Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. Every recursive function must have a **base case** to stop the execution and prevent infinite loops, followed by a **recursive step** that moves closer to the base case.

It matters because it breaks complex problems (like tree traversals, backtracking, and divide-and-conquer algorithms) into clean, elegant, and manageable sub-problems. It mirrors mathematical induction.

Think of recursion like looking into two facing mirrors: you see an infinite reflection, but each reflection is a slightly smaller copy of the previous one until the image gets too small to see clearly (the base case).
how: Identify the base case: the simplest version of the problem that can be answered directly.
Determine the recursive step: break the main problem down into a smaller sub-problem.
Ensure the argument in the recursive call moves closer to the base case on every step.
Combine or return the result of the recursive call to form the final answer.
keyPoints: Every recursive function requires a base case to avoid a Stack Overflow error.
Each recursive call creates a new frame on the system call stack, consuming O(n) space if depth is n.
Tail recursion is a special case where the recursive call is the absolute last operation, allowing compiler optimizations.
Recursion can always be converted into an iterative approach using an explicit stack.
mistakes: Omitting the base case -> Leads to infinite recursion and a stack overflow crash. Always write and test your base case first.
Not shrinking the input -> Passing the same parameters into the recursive call causes an infinite loop.
Ignoring stack space limits -> Deep recursion on large inputs will exhaust system memory.
theory: What is a base case and why is it mandatory?
A base case is the terminating condition in recursion that stops further self-calls. Without it, the function runs infinitely until the call stack memory is exhausted.
What is the time and space complexity of a standard recursive factorial function?
Time complexity is O(n) because there are n recursive calls. Space complexity is O(n) due to the call stack frames stored for each active call.
What is tail recursion?
Tail recursion occurs when the recursive call is the final operation performed by the function, with no pending operations waiting for its return value.
Can all recursive problems be solved iteratively?
Yes, any recursive algorithm can be implemented iteratively using an explicit stack data structure to mimic the call stack.
What happens when the recursion depth exceeds the stack limit?
It triggers a runtime error known as a Stack Overflow.

dsa.recurrence-relations.explain:
A recurrence relation is an equation that defines a sequence recursively in terms of its preceding values. In data structures and algorithms, it expresses the running time of a recursive algorithm as a function of input size `n`.

It matters because analyzing loops is straightforward, but analyzing recursive code (like Merge Sort or Binary Search) requires translating the branching calls into a mathematical equation to find the asymptotic time complexity (Big-O notation).

Think of it like calculating compound interest or population growth where this year's total depends directly on last year's total plus new additions.
how: Identify the number of recursive sub-problems created by the algorithm (a).
Determine the factor by which the input size is reduced in each sub-problem (b).
Express the cost of dividing the problem and combining the results as a separate function of n, f(n).
Write the relation in the standard form: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).
keyPoints: Common solving techniques include Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, and Master Theorem.
T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) evaluates to O(n) time (common in linear recursion like simple loops).
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) evaluates to O(log n) time (common in Binary Search).
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) evaluates to O(n log n) time (common in Merge Sort).
mistakes: Ignoring the work done outside the recursion -> Always include the extra work term f(n) like merging steps.
Confusing subtraction with division -> T(n-1) implies linear recursion tree height, while T(n/2) implies logarithmic tree height.
Forgetting base cases in recurrence evaluation -> Base cases provide the boundary conditions when summing recursion trees.
dsa.recurrence-relations.syntax: T(n) = a * T(n / b) + O(n^k * log^p(n))

code.src:
Worked Example: Analyzing Binary Search Recurrence
1. Algorithm divides input array in half: n/2 -> b = 2
2. Only 1 half is searched recursively -> a = 1
3. Constant time work is done outside recursion (comparison) -> f(n) = O(1)
4. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
5. Using Master Theorem / Tree: Height = log2(n), Work per level = O(1).
Total Time = O(log n).

theory: What is a recurrence relation?
An equation or inequality that describes an algorithm's running time in terms of its input size on smaller inputs.
What does 'a' represent in T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)?
It represents the number of sub-problems created in the recursive step.
What does 'b' represent in the standard recurrence equation?
It is the factor by which the input size is reduced for each sub-problem.
What is the recursion tree method?
A visual technique where the recurrence is expanded into a tree, and the total cost is calculated by summing the costs of all nodes across all levels.
What is the difference between T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n and T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1?
The first represents a divide-and-conquer approach running in O(n log n), while the second represents a deep linear recursive tree running in exponential O(2^n) time.
coding: Apply Master Theorem: a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = n. n^(log_b(a)) = n^(log_2(4)) = n^2. Since f(n) = O(n) is polynomially smaller than n^2 (Case 1), T(n) = Theta(n^2).
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), where 2 is the two halves, n/2 is the halved input size, and O(n) is the linear time merging cost.
Solve Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n

Use the recursion tree method. The tree depth is unbalanced, ranging from log_3(n) to log_{3/2}(n). Total work per level is c*n, and the tree height is O(n), leading to O(n log n) overall time complexity.

dsa.master-theorem.explain:
The Master Theorem is a cookbook formula used to quickly determine the time complexity of divide-and-conquer recurrence relations of the form **T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)**, without drawing cumbersome recursion trees.

It matters because in competitive programming, systems design, and technical interviews, you need to analyze divide-and-conquer algorithms (like Merge Sort, Strassen's Matrix Multiplication, or Fast Fourier Transform) instantly.

Think of it like a quick chemical test: instead of analyzing every molecule in a compound, you apply three quick rule checks to instantly identify which category it belongs to.
how: Extract parameters `a`, `b`, and function `f(n)` from the recurrence relation T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).
Calculate the critical exponent $c_{crit} = \log_b(a)$.
Compare $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b(a)}$ to see which function grows faster.
Match the relation to Case 1, Case 2, or Case 3 of the Master Theorem to write down the final asymptotic bound.
keyPoints: Case 1: If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b(a) - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)}).$
Case 2: If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)} \log^k n)$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)} \log^{k+1} n).$
Case 3: If $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b(a) + \epsilon})$ and regularity condition holds, then $T(n) = \Theta(f(n)).$
The Master Theorem does not apply if the gap between $f(n)$ and $n^{\log_b(a)}$ is non-polynomial (e.g., logarithmic factor mismatch not covered by Case 2).
mistakes: Trying to apply it to non-divide-and-conquer relations -> It does not work for subtractive recurrences like T(n) = T(n-1) + n.
Confusing polynomial dominance -> Forgetting that inequalities must hold by a polynomial factor (epsilon > 0) in cases 1 and 3.
Miscalculating $\log_b(a)$ -> Double-check base-b logs, especially when b is not 2.

code.src:
Worked Example: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n
1. Identify: a = 9, b = 3, f(n) = n
2. Compute critical exponent: log_b(a) = log_3(9) = 2
3. Compare f(n) = n with n^(log_b(a)) = n^2
4. Since n is polynomially smaller than n^2 (n = O(n^(2-1))), this falls under Case 1.
5. Result: T(n) = Theta(n^2)

theory: What is the primary purpose of the Master Theorem?
To provide a quick asymptotic solution for divide-and-conquer recurrence relations of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).
What are the prerequisites for applying the Master Theorem?
The sub-problems must be of equal size (n/b), work must be divided evenly, and f(n) must be asymptotically positive.
When does the Master Theorem fail to provide an answer?
It fails when f(n) and n^(log_b(a)) are not polynomially comparable (e.g., when f(n) is smaller by a polylogarithmic factor instead of a strict polynomial factor).
What does Case 2 of the Master Theorem state?
If the work at the leaves and root are balanced (f(n) matches n^(log_b(a))), the total cost multiplies by a logarithmic factor log n.
Can the Master Theorem solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n?
Yes, this falls under Case 2 with k=1, yielding T(n) = Theta(n log^2 n).
coding: a=8, b=2, f(n)=n^2. log_2(8) = 3. Compare n^2 with n^3. f(n) is smaller (Case 1: n^2 = O(n^(3-1))). Result: Theta(n^3).
a=1, b=2, f(n)=1. log_2(1) = 0. n^0 = 1. f(n) = Theta(n^0), matching Case 2 with k=0. Result: Theta(log n).
a=3, b=4, f(n)=n log n. log_4(3) approx 0.793. Since n log n is strictly greater than n^0.793 by a polynomial factor (epsilon), Case 3 applies. Result: Theta(n log n).

dsa.rotate-array.explain:
- **What it is**: Array rotation means shifting all elements of an array by *k* positions. The *reversal algorithm* does this in‑place using three simple reversals, avoiding extra memory.
- **Why it matters**: Many interview problems (e.g., cyclic shifts, string manipulation, buffer handling) require O(1) extra space and O(n) time. The three‑reverse method meets both constraints.
- **Real‑life analogy**: Imagine a circular conveyor belt with boxes. To move every box *k* steps forward, you can first flip the whole belt, then flip the first *k* boxes, and finally flip the remaining boxes – the belt ends up looking exactly as if each box moved forward *k* spots.
- **Key insight**: Reversing a segment of an array reverses the order of its elements. By chaining reversals you can change the direction of a segment without moving each element individually.
how: 1. Normalize k: k = k % n (n = array length) to handle k > n and negative k.
2. Reverse the whole array: `reverse(arr, 0, n-1)`.
3. Reverse the first k elements: `reverse(arr, 0, k-1)`.
4. Reverse the remaining n‑k elements: `reverse(arr, k, n-1)`.
5. The array is now rotated right by k positions (left rotation uses n‑k).
keyPoints: Time complexity O(n), space O(1).
Works for both right and left rotations (use n‑k for left).
Normalization (k % n) prevents unnecessary full cycles.
The three reversals are in‑place using std::swap.
Works for any data type as long as swap is defined.
mistakes: Using k instead of k % n – leads to extra work or out‑of‑bounds errors.
Reversing in wrong order (e.g., reversing first segment before whole array) gives incorrect result.
For left rotation, forgetting to convert k to n‑k causes opposite direction.
Calling reverse with wrong indices (off‑by‑one) – ensure inclusive bounds.
dsa.rotate-array.syntax: void reverse(T arr[], int l, int r) { while (l < r) swap(arr[l++], arr[r--]); }
theory: Explain the three‑step reversal algorithm for array rotation.
First reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, finally reverse the remaining n‑k elements. This yields a right rotation by k.
Why do we use k % n before rotating?
To eliminate full cycles; rotating by n or multiples of n leaves the array unchanged and prevents index overflow.
Can the algorithm rotate left? How?
Yes, left rotation by k is equivalent to right rotation by n‑k, or you can reverse whole array then reverse last k elements and then first n‑k.
What is the space complexity and why?
O(1) because we only use a few integer variables and swap in‑place; no auxiliary array is allocated.
How does this method compare to the naive O(k·n) shift?
The naive method moves each element one step k times → O(k·n). The reversal method moves each element at most twice → O(n).
coding: Rotate an array of size N by K positions to the right using the reversal algorithm.
Given an array, rotate it left by K positions without extra space.
Find the minimum number of right rotations needed to make a sorted array become strictly decreasing.

dsa.difference-array.explain:
A **Difference Array** is an auxiliary array used to efficiently perform multiple range update queries (adding a value `x` to all elements from index `L` to `R`) in `O(1)` time per update. Instead of updating every element in the range one by one (which takes `O(N)`), we only modify two elements in the difference array: add `x` at index `L` and subtract `x` at index `R + 1`.

After all updates are processed, we compute the prefix sum of the difference array to get the final updated array in `O(N)` time. This technique turns multiple expensive range updates into a single prefix sum sweep at the end, drastically improving efficiency from `O(N 	imes Q)` to `O(N + Q)`.

Think of it like a ledger of salary adjustments. Instead of rewriting everyone's salary every month, you only note down the *change* (raise) at the employee where the raise starts, and a *cancellation* (minus raise) right after the employee where the raise stops. At the end of the year, running a running-total (prefix sum) from the beginning reveals everyone's exact current salary.
how: Create a difference array `diff` of size `N + 1` initialized to all zeros.
For each range update `[L, R]` with value `Val`, do `diff[L] += Val` and `diff[R + 1] -= Val`.
After all queries are applied, compute the prefix sum array from `diff`.
Add the prefix sum values to the original array elements to get the final result.
keyPoints: Reduces range update time complexity from `O(N)` to `O(1)`.
Requires `O(N)` final processing step using prefix sums.
Size of the difference array should be `N + 1` to safely handle updates up to index `N - 1`.
Works only for additive updates; does not support range multiplications directly without logarithms.
Essential technique for competitive programming and interval-based scheduling problems.
mistakes: Forgetting to size the difference array to `N + 1`, leading to segmentation faults on `diff[R + 1]` -> Always allocate `N + 1` elements.
Confusing range updates with range query outputs -> Difference array is for updates, Fenwick/Segment trees are for fast queries.
Applying prefix sum before all queries are completed -> Accumulate all updates first, then run the prefix sum once.
theory: What is the time complexity of range updates using a difference array?
O(1) per update query.
Why do we need an array of size N + 1?
To handle updates that extend up to index N - 1 without causing an out-of-bounds error when subtracting at R + 1.
Can difference arrays handle range minimum or maximum queries?
No, difference arrays are designed for cumulative sum range updates, not range extrema queries.
How do you combine range updates and point queries?
Apply all updates to the difference array and take the prefix sum up to the queried index.
Is a difference array useful for offline or online queries?
It is primarily an offline technique because all updates are applied first, followed by a single prefix sum pass.
coding: // Use difference array to record seat reservations across flight ranges [first, last] and compute prefix sum at the end.
// Map passenger capacity changes along road locations using a difference array and check if capacity exceeds limits.

dsa.kadane.explain:
A **Kadane's Algorithm** is an iterative dynamic programming algorithm used to find the maximum contiguous subarray sum within a one-dimensional numeric array in `O(N)` time. Instead of checking all possible subarrays (which takes `O(N^2)` or `O(N^3)`), Kadane's algorithm scans the array while maintaining two values: the maximum sum ending at the current position (`curr_sum`) and the global maximum sum found so far (`max_sum`).

At each step, the algorithm decides whether to extend the previous subarray by including the current element, or to start a fresh subarray from the current element if the previous sum has dropped below zero. This greedy property allows it to discard negative weight prefixes instantly.

Imagine walking down a path collecting gold coins (positive numbers) and paying tolls (negative numbers). If your total pocket money drops below zero, holding onto that debt is pointless; you are better off dropping your bag and starting fresh with the next coin you find. The maximum amount of money you ever had in your pocket at any single point is your Kadane maximum.
how: Initialize `curr_sum = 0` and `max_sum = INT_MIN` (or `arr[0]`).
Iterate through each element `x` of the array.
Update `curr_sum = max(x, curr_sum + x)` (decide whether to start fresh or extend).
Update `max_sum = max(max_sum, curr_sum)`.
Return `max_sum` after the loop finishes.
keyPoints: Time complexity: `O(N)` single pass; Space complexity: `O(1)` auxiliary space.
Fails if all elements are negative unless explicitly handled (initialize `max_sum` to the first element and `curr_sum = 0`).
Belongs to the dynamic programming and greedy paradigm families.
Can be modified to return the start and end indices of the maximum subarray.
Widely asked in entry-level and mid-level tech interviews.
mistakes: Initializing `max_sum` to `0` instead of `INT_MIN` or `arr[0]` -> Fails if all numbers in the array are negative.
Forgetting to handle arrays with a single element -> Ensure base cases are checked.
Resetting `curr_sum` to `0` instead of taking `max(x, curr_sum + x)` -> Fails when all numbers are negative.
theory: What is the time and space complexity of Kadane's algorithm?
O(N) time and O(1) space.
How does Kadane's algorithm handle all-negative arrays?
If max_sum is initialized to the first element and curr_sum starts at 0, it correctly returns the single maximum negative element.
Can Kadane's algorithm be used for circular arrays?
Yes, by running standard Kadane and also finding the minimum subarray sum to subtract from the total array sum.
What design paradigm does Kadane's algorithm use?
It is a classic example of Dynamic Programming optimized down to O(1) space, and can also be viewed through a greedy lens.
How would you retrieve the start and end indices of the max subarray?
Keep track of temporary start indices and update the best start/end pointers whenever max_sum is updated.
coding: // Standard implementation of Kadane's algorithm returning the max sum.
// Total sum minus minimum subarray sum, handled with edge cases for all negative arrays.

dsa.dutch-flag.explain:
The **Dutch National Flag Algorithm** (invented by Edsger Dijkstra) is an efficient three-pointer partitioning algorithm used to sort an array containing elements of only three distinct values (typically `0`, `1`, and `2`) in a single pass of `O(N)` time and `O(1)` space.

The algorithm uses three pointers: `low` (boundary for `0`), `mid` (current scanning element), and `high` (boundary for `2`). As `mid` traverses the array, it inspects each element and swaps it into its correct partition region: values of `0` are swapped with `low`, values of `2` are swapped with `high`, and values of `1` are simply bypassed by advancing `mid`.

Imagine sorting a mixed pile of red, white, and blue balls into three neat sections. You hold a scanner in your hand (`mid`). If you see red, you throw it to the red zone on the left (`low`). If you see blue, you throw it to the blue zone on the right (`high`). If you see white, you leave it in the middle zone and move on. When your scanner meets the blue zone pointer, all balls are perfectly sorted.
how: Initialize pointer `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, and `high = n - 1`.
While `mid <= high`, examine the element at `arr[mid]`.
If `arr[mid] == 0`, swap `arr[low]` and `arr[mid]`, then increment both `low` and `mid`.
If `arr[mid] == 1`, just increment `mid`.
If `arr[mid] == 2`, swap `arr[mid]` and `arr[high]`, then decrement `high` (do not increment `mid` yet).
keyPoints: Sorting takes exactly `O(N)` time with a single traversal.
Requires `O(1)` auxiliary space.
Partition invariant: elements before `low` are `0`, elements after `high` are `2`, elements between `low` and `mid` are `1`.
Extremely common in technical interviews for array manipulation problems.
Works for any problem requiring partitioning an array into three categories.
mistakes: Incrementing `mid` after swapping with `high` -> Incorrect, because the swapped element from `high` has not been inspected yet and needs evaluation.
Incorrect pointer initialization (`high` set to `n` instead of `n - 1`) -> Causes out-of-bounds errors.
Confusing partition boundaries -> Remember that `mid` is the active scanner exploring unknown territory.
theory: Why is mid not incremented when swapping with high?
Because the element swapped from high is unexamined and must be processed by the mid pointer in the next iteration.
What are the loop termination conditions for the Dutch National Flag algorithm?
The loop terminates when mid exceeds high (mid > high).
What is the space complexity of this algorithm?
O(1) auxiliary space as sorting is performed in-place.
Can this algorithm be generalized for K distinct values?
Yes, though it turns into multi-way partitioning or counting sort depending on constraints.
Who invented the Dutch National Flag problem?
Edsger Dijkstra.
coding: // Implement the standard 3-pointer Dutch National Flag algorithm to sort 0s, 1s, and 2s.
// Standard GFG / LeetCode variation requiring in-place sorting in one pass.

dsa.two-pointers.explain:
The Two Pointers technique involves using two integer indices (or pointers) to iterate through a data structure—usually an array or string—often moving towards each other from both ends, or moving in the same direction at different speeds. It transforms naive $O(n^2)$ nested loop algorithms into efficient $O(n)$ linear time solutions.

This matters immensely in campus placements (at companies like TCS, Wipro, and product-based firms visiting Gurugram/NCR) because array searching and string manipulation questions frequently demand optimal space and time complexities.

Think of two people meeting in the middle of a long hallway: instead of one person walking back and forth checking every single spot, they start at opposite ends and walk towards each other based on clues, meeting quickly in the middle.
how: Initialize two pointers, say `left = 0` and `right = n - 1`, for a sorted array.
Evaluate the condition or sum formed by the elements at `left` and `right`.
If the condition is met, record the result or adjust indices.
If the sum is too small, increment `left` to increase the value.
If the sum is too large, decrement `right` to decrease the value.
Repeat until `left >= right`.
keyPoints: Array or string must typically be sorted beforehand for opposite-direction pointers.
Time Complexity: $O(n)$ because each element is visited at most once by each pointer.
Space Complexity: $O(1)$ auxiliary space as no extra data structures are used.
Extremely useful for Pair Sum, 3Sum, Palindrome checks, and Container With Most Water problems.
C++ Standard: C++20/C++23 features like `std::ranges` can sometimes encapsulate these patterns, but manual indexing remains standard.
mistakes: Forgetting to sort the array beforehand -> Always verify if the input array is sorted.
Infinite loops due to incorrect pointer increments/decrements -> Ensure `left` and `right` strictly move closer.
Out-of-bounds errors -> Check boundary conditions like `left < right` versus `left <= right`.
theory: What is the primary condition for using opposite-direction Two Pointers?
The array or data structure is usually required to be sorted.
What is the time complexity of the Two Pointers technique?
O(n) time complexity since each element is examined at most once by each pointer.
Can Two Pointers be used on unsorted arrays?
Yes, but typically for in-place modifications (like removing duplicates or partitioning) rather than search-based sum problems.
How does Two Pointers differ from Sliding Window?
Two Pointers usually involve two ends closing in or moving independently, whereas Sliding Window maintains a range/window of elements moving in the same direction.
What is the space complexity?
O(1) auxiliary space.
Is Two Pointers applicable to linked lists?
Yes, e.g., finding the middle element or detecting cycles using fast and slow pointers.
coding: Use two pointers, one at the start and one at the end, moving inward while skipping non-alphanumeric characters.
Swap characters at `left` and `right` indices, then increment `left` and decrement `right`.
Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
Apply standard opposite-direction pointers to find indices that add up to target.

dsa.sliding-window.explain:
The Sliding Window technique is used to perform operations on a specific subset (window) of data in a large array or string, sliding that window across the data structure step-by-step. Instead of recomputing results for overlapping sub-arrays from scratch ($O(n^2)$), it updates the window in $O(1)$ time by adding the new element entering the window and removing the old element leaving it.

This matters because interviewers at product companies frequently test your ability to optimize substring or subarray problems from $O(n^2)$ or $O(n^3)$ down to $O(n)$.

Imagine looking through a moving train window at a scenic landscape: as the train moves forward, new scenery enters your view on one side while old scenery disappears from the other side, rather than you having to walk through the entire train to look out a different window every second.
how: Identify whether the problem asks for subarrays/substrings of a fixed size or a variable size based on a condition.
Initialize pointers (e.g., `start = 0`, `end = 0`) to represent the window boundaries.
Expand the window by moving the `end` pointer and updating the window state/sum.
For variable-size windows, shrink the window from the `start` when the condition is violated.
Track and update the maximum or minimum result at each valid window state.
Continue until the `end` pointer reaches the end of the array.
keyPoints: Fixed-Size Window: The window size $k$ is constant; slide by adding `arr[i]` and removing `arr[i - k]`.
Variable-Size Window: Window size expands and contracts dynamically based on constraints.
Time Complexity: $O(n)$ since every element enters and leaves the window at most once.
Space Complexity: $O(1)$ or $O(k)$ depending on whether hash maps/sets are used for tracking counts.
Widely applicable for problems involving max/min sums, longest substring without repeating characters, etc.
mistakes: Recalculating the window aggregate from scratch at every step -> Always update incrementally.
Incorrect boundary updates for variable windows -> Ensure the `while` loop condition for shrinking is robust.
Off-by-one errors in fixed window sizing -> Make sure window size equals `end - start + 1`.
theory: What is the main advantage of Sliding Window over brute force?
It reduces time complexity from O(n*k) or O(n^2) to O(n).
What are the two main types of sliding windows?
Fixed-size window and Variable-size window.
When should you use a variable-size sliding window?
When the problem asks for the longest/shortest subarray/substring that satisfies a specific condition (e.g., sum <= target).
What is the time complexity for processing elements in a sliding window?
O(n) because each element is processed at most twice (once by `end`, once by `start`).
How do you handle character frequency tracking in strings?
Using an array of size 256 or an unordered_map inside the window.
Can sliding window be applied to negative numbers?
For variable-size windows requiring a exact sum, negative numbers break monotonic properties; prefix sums with hash maps are preferred there.
coding: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
Use a fixed-size sliding window of size k, updating sum in O(1).
Use a variable-size sliding window with a hash set/map to store character indices.
Use a variable-size sliding window to find the minimal length whose sum is greater than or equal to target.

dsa.moores-voting.explain:
Moore’s Voting Algorithm is an ingenious linear-time algorithm designed to find the majority element in an array—an element that appears strictly more than $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ times. It works by maintaining a candidate element and a counter, incrementing when matching the candidate and decrementing when encountering a different element, effectively canceling out non-majority elements.

This is a classic interview favorite because it tests whether a student knows how to achieve optimal $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space without resorting to sorting ($O(n \log n)$) or hash maps ($O(n)$ space).

Imagine a political election where voters represent array elements: if a candidate has absolute majority support (more than 50%), even if all opposing candidates team up to cancel out votes pairwise, the majority candidate will still have leftover votes at the end.
how: Initialize `candidate = -1` and `count = 0`.
Iterate through each element `num` in the array:
If `count == 0`, set `candidate = num` and set `count = 1`.
Else if `num == candidate`, increment `count` by 1.
Else, decrement `count` by 1.
After the loop, the `candidate` variable holds the potential majority element. (Optional verification pass: count its occurrences to confirm it exceeds $n/2$).
keyPoints: Time Complexity: $O(n)$ since it requires only one pass (plus an optional second pass for verification).
Space Complexity: $O(1)$ auxiliary space as it only stores two variables (`candidate` and `count`).
Only works if a majority element guaranteed to appear $> n/2$ times actually exists (otherwise verification step is mandatory).
Failing to verify when no majority element exists is a common trap in coding interviews.
Extremely elegant demonstration of state tracking with constant memory.
mistakes: Assuming the algorithm always returns the correct majority element when none exists -> Always run a second verification pass if existence isn't guaranteed.
Confusing count decrement with resetting the candidate prematurely -> Count must hit 0 before switching candidates.
Applying it to problems requiring elements appearing $> n/3$ times without modifying it to two candidates (Boyer-Moore Majority Vote extension).
theory: What is the time and space complexity of Moore’s Voting Algorithm?
O(n) time and O(1) space.
What condition must be met for a majority element to exist?
It must appear strictly more than n / 2 times in the array.
Why is the verification step necessary?
If the input array does not contain a true majority element, the algorithm will still output a candidate, which must be verified.
Can Moore’s Voting Algorithm find elements appearing > n/3 times?
Not directly, but the Boyer-Moore voting algorithm can be extended to track two candidates for n/3 problems.
How does the cancellation logic work?
Non-majority elements cancel out majority elements; because the majority count > n/2, it survives.
What happens if all elements are distinct?
The count will drop to 0 repeatedly, and the last element processed will be returned as candidate (which fails verification).
coding: Implement Moore's Voting Algorithm to find the element appearing > n/2 times.
Extend the voting algorithm to find all elements that appear more than n/3 times using two candidates.
Check Majority Element in Sorted Array
Use binary search or two pointers to count frequency in O(log n).

dsa.kmp.explain:
- **What it is**: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm finds all occurrences of a pattern string *P* of length *m* inside a text string *T* of length *n* in linear time *O(n+m)*.
- **Why it matters**: Naïve search may re‑compare characters many times, leading to *O(n·m)* in the worst case. KMP avoids this by pre‑computing a **Longest Prefix‑Suffix (LPS)** array that tells how far the pattern can shift without re‑examining characters.
- **Real‑life analogy**: Imagine scanning a tape for a word. When a mismatch occurs, instead of rewinding the tape to the start, you remember how much of the word you already matched and continue from the longest possible prefix that is also a suffix.
- The algorithm consists of two phases: building the LPS array for the pattern, then scanning the text using the LPS to skip unnecessary comparisons.
- It is a staple in interview questions on string matching and appears in many real‑world tools like text editors, DNA sequence analysis, and intrusion‑detection systems.
how: 1. Compute the LPS (prefix function) array for the pattern in O(m) time.
2. Initialise two indices i (for text) and j (for pattern) at 0.
3. While i < n, compare T[i] with P[j].
4. If they match, increment both i and j. If j reaches m, report a match and set j = LPS[j‑1].
5. If a mismatch occurs and j > 0, set j = LPS[j‑1] (no i increment). Otherwise increment i.
keyPoints: LPS[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix.
Total time complexity is O(n+m); space O(m) for LPS.
Works for any alphabet; case‑sensitive by default.
When a mismatch happens, KMP never moves i backwards.
Useful for multiple pattern searches when combined with automata (Aho‑Corasick).
mistakes: Computing LPS incorrectly – forgetting the "proper" prefix condition; fix by resetting length to LPS[length‑1] on mismatch.
Using j = 0 after a match instead of LPS[m‑1]; you lose overlapping matches.
Assuming KMP is faster for very short strings – overhead of LPS may dominate; choose naïve for tiny inputs.
Forgetting to reset j after a mismatch when j==0; you must increment i.
Mixing 0‑based and 1‑based indices; keep everything 0‑based in C++ implementation.

code.out:
Match at index 0
Match at index 5
Match at index 10

theory: What is the purpose of the LPS array in KMP?
It stores the length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix for each prefix, enabling the algorithm to skip re‑checking characters after a mismatch.
State the worst‑case time complexity of KMP and why it is linear.
O(n+m) because each character of the text and pattern is examined at most twice – once during the forward scan and possibly once during a fallback via LPS.
How does KMP handle overlapping pattern occurrences?
After reporting a match, j is set to LPS[m‑1] instead of 0, allowing the next possible match to start inside the previous match.
Can KMP be used for multiple patterns simultaneously?
Not directly; for multiple patterns use Aho‑Corasick, but KMP can be run repeatedly for each pattern.
Why does KMP never move the text index i backwards?
The LPS array tells exactly how many characters of the pattern are already matched, so the algorithm can shift the pattern right without revisiting earlier text characters.
What is a ‘proper’ prefix?
A prefix that is not equal to the whole string; e.g., for "abc", "ab" is proper, "abc" is not.
coding: Find all occurrences of a pattern in a given text (Easy)
Use the KMP implementation above; read two strings, output indices separated by space.
Given a DNA sequence (string of A,C,G,T) and a motif, count overlapping occurrences (Medium)
Apply KMP; after each match, continue with j = LPS[m-1] to count overlaps.
Replace every occurrence of a pattern in a text with another string using KMP for search (Hard)
First locate all start indices with KMP, then rebuild the result string by copying segments and inserting the replacement.

dsa.merge-intervals.explain:
The **Merge Intervals** problem requires taking a collection of intervals, where each interval is represented as a start and end time `[start, end]`, and merging all overlapping intervals.

This pattern matters immensely in technical interviews (LeetCode 56) and real-world systems like calendar scheduling, CPU task allocation, and database indexing. 

Think of it like planning a day with multiple overlapping meetings: if Meeting A runs from 9:00 to 10:30 and Meeting B runs from 10:00 to 11:00, you combine them into a single continuous block from 9:00 to 11:00.
how: Sort the intervals array based on the starting value of each interval in ascending order.
Initialize a result data structure (like a vector of vectors) and push the first interval into it.
Iterate through the remaining intervals one by one.
Compare the current interval's start time with the last interval's end time in the result list.
If they overlap (current start <= last end), update the last interval's end time to be the maximum of both end times.
If they do not overlap, simply append the current interval to the result list.
keyPoints: Sorting is the crucial first step; without it, checking all pairs takes O(n^2) time.
Time complexity is dominated by sorting: O(n log n).
Space complexity is O(n) to store the merged intervals output.
Two intervals `[a, b]` and `[c, d]` overlap if `c <= b` (assuming sorted starts).
Frequently asked in top product-based company interviews.
mistakes: Forgetting to sort the intervals first -> Always sort by the start time.
Modifying intervals in place without handling vector resizing correctly -> Use a separate result container.
Using `min` instead of `max` for the end time when merging -> Ensure the end time extends as far as needed.
theory: What is the time complexity of the merge intervals algorithm?
O(n log n) due to sorting, where n is the number of intervals. The merge pass itself takes O(n).
How do you know if two intervals overlap?
If interval A starts before or when interval B ends, and interval B starts before or when interval A ends.
Can this be solved without sorting?
Not efficiently. Without sorting, comparing every pair takes O(n^2) time.
What if the input intervals are already sorted?
Then the time complexity drops to O(n) since we only need a single linear scan.
How do you handle edge cases like a single interval?
The algorithm checks if the input is empty and handles single intervals naturally by returning them unchanged.
coding: Given a set of non-overlapping intervals, insert a new interval into the intervals (merge if necessary).
Given an array of meeting time intervals consisting of start and end times, find the minimum number of conference rooms required.
Given an array of intervals, find the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

dsa.matrix-rotation.explain:
Matrix manipulation problems, such as **Rotating a Matrix by 90 degrees** or traversing it in a **Spiral Order**, test your 2D array indexing and spatial reasoning skills.

In C++, 2D vectors or arrays are stored in row-major order. Rotating a matrix 90 degrees clockwise can be elegantly achieved in-place using two fundamental matrix operations: **transposing** the matrix (swapping rows and columns) and then **reversing each row**.

Imagine turning a physical sheet of paper with text on it: instead of recalculating every new coordinate complexly, you flip it diagonally (transpose) and then flip it horizontally (reverse rows).
how: Check if the matrix is empty or not square (for 90-degree rotation, it must be an N x N matrix).
Perform the Transpose operation by swapping element `matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]` for all `i < j`.
Iterate through each row of the transposed matrix.
Reverse the elements of each row using `std::reverse`.
The matrix is now successfully rotated 90 degrees clockwise in-place.
keyPoints: In-place 90-degree rotation requires O(1) extra space.
Time complexity for transpose and reverse is O(N^2), where N is the number of rows/columns.
Transpose step only loops through the upper or lower triangle (`j` starts from `i+1`).
Spiral matrix traversal uses four boundaries (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`) to navigate layer by layer.
Crucial for graphics programming, image processing, and game development.

dsa.string-basics.explain:
Strings are fundamental data structures used to store sequences of characters. In C++, `std::string` manages dynamic character arrays under the hood, handling memory allocation and resizing automatically.

Unlike languages like Java or Python where strings are strictly immutable, `std::string` in C++ is **mutable**, meaning you can modify individual characters in-place. However, understanding string manipulation, passing strings by reference to avoid expensive copying, and using efficient building techniques is critical for performance.

Think of a string like a beaded necklace: modifying a mutable string is like swapping out a single bead, whereas creating new strings repeatedly is like tearing down the necklace and stringing a brand new one from scratch every time.
how: Include the `<string>` header in your C++ program.
Declare strings using `std::string s = "hello";`.
Modify characters directly using indexing like `s[0] = 'H';`.
Pass strings to functions by reference (`const string& s` for reading, `string& s` for modifying) to prevent unnecessary deep copies.
Use `.length()` or `.size()` to find the number of characters and `.append()` or `+` operator for concatenation.
keyPoints: `std::string` is mutable in C++, unlike Java's `String` class.
Always pass large strings by reference (`const string&`) in function parameters to avoid O(N) copy overhead.
C-style strings are null-terminated character arrays (`char[]`), which are prone to buffer overflows if not handled carefully.
Time complexity of random access `s[i]` is O(1).
Appending to a string can trigger reallocation, taking amortized O(1) time.
mistakes: Passing large strings by value into functions -> Causes costly O(N) memory duplication. Always use references.
Assuming C++ `std::string` is null-terminated internally for safety while ignoring raw pointer decays -> Use `.c_str()` when interacting with C APIs.
Using `==` incorrectly on C-style char arrays instead of `strcmp` -> In C++, `std::string` overloads `==` properly, but char pointers just compare memory addresses.
theory: Are strings in C++ mutable?
Yes, C++ `std::string` objects are mutable, allowing characters to be changed in-place.
Why should you pass strings by `const string&` in functions?
To avoid the performance overhead of copying the entire string data in memory.
What is the difference between `std::string` and C-style strings?
`std::string` is a dynamic, safe C++ standard library class that manages its own memory, whereas C-style strings are static char arrays terminated by a null character `\0`.
What is the time complexity of accessing a character by index in `std::string`?
O(1) constant time, as it uses direct pointer/array offset indexing.
How do you convert a `std::string` to a C-style null-terminated string?
By using the `.c_str()` member function.

dsa.palindrome.explain:
A palindrome is a string, word, number, or other sequence of characters that reads the same forward and backward (ignoring spaces, punctuation, and capitalization in real-world use, though exact matching is common in basic DSA problems).

In data structures and algorithms, checking for a palindrome is a fundamental string manipulation exercise. It tests your ability to navigate indices and manipulate pointers.

It matters in interviews because it's a staple warmup problem that evaluates your grasp of array indexing, two-pointer techniques, and space-time optimization.

Think of a palindrome like looking into a mirror where the reflection spells out the exact same word. If you place a finger at the start and end of the word and move them inward, they should always land on matching characters.
how: Initialize two pointers: `left` at index 0 and `right` at index `n - 1`.
Loop while `left` is less than `right`.
Compare the character at `left` with the character at `right`.
If they don't match, return false (not a palindrome).
If they match, increment `left` and decrement `right`, then repeat.
If the loop finishes without mismatches, return true.
keyPoints: Two-pointer approach achieves O(N) time complexity.
Space complexity is O(1) as no extra storage is needed.
Always handle edge cases like empty strings or single-character strings.
In C++, strings are mutable, making indexing straightforward.
Watch out for case sensitivity and special characters if required by the problem statement.
mistakes: Allocating a new reversed string and comparing it -> Fix: Use the two-pointer approach to avoid O(N) extra space.
Off-by-one errors in pointer bounds -> Fix: Ensure loop condition is `left < right` rather than `left <= right` (though both work, `left < right` saves an unnecessary self-comparison).
Forgetting to handle empty strings -> Fix: Empty strings are typically considered palindromes by definition; check constraints first.
theory: What is the time and space complexity of the optimal palindrome check?
Time complexity is O(N) where N is the string length, and space complexity is O(1).
Can we solve this using recursion?
Yes, by comparing outer characters and recursively calling the function on the substring excluding the first and last characters.
How do you handle palindromes with spaces and punctuation?
You preprocess the string by filtering out non-alphanumeric characters and converting everything to lowercase before applying the two-pointer check.
Is an integer palindrome check different from a string check?
For integers, you can either convert to string or mathematically reverse the integer digits and compare.
Why use two pointers instead of reversing the string?
Reversing the string creates a copy taking O(N) extra memory, whereas two pointers operate in-place with O(1) space.
coding: Expand around center approach: check all 2N-1 possible centers (each char and space between chars) and expand outward while characters match.
Find the middle of the linked list using slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, and compare with the first half.

dsa.anagram.explain:
An anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once. For example, 'listen' and 'silent' are anagrams.

In DSA, checking for anagrams tests your understanding of frequency counting, hashing, and sorting.

It matters in interviews because it evaluates your ability to optimize from an O(N log N) sorting approach down to an optimal O(N) frequency counting approach using arrays or hash maps.

Think of it like taking two bowls of letter soup. If both bowls contain the exact same count of each alphabet tile, they are anagrams, regardless of the order you picked them out.
how: Check if the lengths of both strings are equal; if not, they cannot be anagrams.
Initialize a frequency array or hash map of size 26 (for lowercase English letters) with all zeros.
Iterate through the first string and increment the count for each character.
Iterate through the second string and decrement the count for each character.
Check if all counts in the frequency array/map are zero.
Return true if all are zero, otherwise false.
keyPoints: Array of size 26 is faster and uses less memory than a hash map for standard lowercase English letters.
Time complexity of the frequency array method is O(N), where N is the length of the string.
Space complexity is O(1) because the frequency array size is constant (26).
Sorting both strings takes O(N log N) time and is an alternative simpler implementation.
Always check string length equality first as an early exit optimization.
mistakes: Comparing sorted strings when length check fails -> Fix: Always check if `s1.length() != s2.length()` first.
Using a complex hash map when a fixed-size integer array suffices -> Fix: Use `int freq[26] = {0};` for lowercase letters to save overhead.
Forgetting to handle case sensitivity -> Fix: Convert all characters to lowercase or uppercase before counting frequencies.
theory: What is the time complexity of checking anagrams using sorting?
O(N log N) due to the sorting algorithm.
What is the time complexity using a frequency array?
O(N) since we traverse the strings a constant number of times.
Why is an array preferred over a hash map for ASCII/lowercase letters?
An array has O(1) direct index access with zero collision overhead and minimal memory footprint.
How would you handle Unicode or international characters?
Use a hash map (like `std::unordered_map<char, int>` in C++) instead of a fixed array of size 26.
What is an interview follow-up if strings are extremely large and stream-based?
You can use character frequency hashing or prime number multiplication, though overflow issues must be managed.
coding: Use the frequency array technique shown in the code section above.

Use a sliding window of size equal to the pattern length combined with a frequency array comparison.

dsa.string-matching.explain:
String matching is the problem of finding occurrences of a pattern string `P` of length `m` within a larger text string `T` of length `n`.

The Naive String Matching algorithm works by aligning the pattern at every possible index of the text and checking character by character.

It matters in interviews because it establishes the baseline brute-force approach before discussing advanced algorithms like KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt), Rabin-Karp, or Z-algorithm.

Imagine looking for a specific 3-letter word in a dictionary. You place your finger at the start of the page, check if the first letters match, then slide your finger one position to the right and repeat until you check the entire page.
how: Loop through the text `T` from index `i = 0` to `n - m`.
For each position `i`, initialize a nested loop to compare text characters `T[i + j]` with pattern characters `P[j]` where `j` goes from `0` to `m - 1`.
If a mismatch is found, break out of the inner loop.
If the inner loop completes successfully (i.e., `j == m`), record `i` as a valid match position.
Continue until all starting positions in `T` are checked.
keyPoints: Worst-case time complexity is O((n - m + 1) * m), which simplifies to O(nm).
Best-case time complexity is O(n) when the first character of the pattern frequently mismatches.
Space complexity is O(1) as no extra data structures are required.
Inefficient for large texts and patterns because it rechecks characters unnecessarily.
Serves as the foundation for understanding why advanced pattern-matching algorithms are needed.
mistakes: Off-by-one error in loop bounds -> Fix: Outer loop must run up to `n - m`, not `n`, to prevent buffer overflow.
Not resetting inner loop variables correctly -> Fix: Ensure index tracking for the pattern starts at 0 for every new text position.
Assuming built-in functions like `find()` are naive -> Fix: Standard library functions use optimized algorithms like Boyer-Moore or Two-Way, not naive search.

Give a worst-case scenario example for Naive String Matching.

Why do we loop up to `n - m` instead of `n` in the outer loop?
Because if the remaining text is shorter than the pattern, a match is impossible.
What are some advanced string matching algorithms that improve upon naive search?
KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt), Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, and Z-Algorithm.
What is the main advantage of the Naive approach despite its O(nm) complexity?
Simplicity of implementation, zero extra space required (O(1)), and high efficiency for short strings or random text.

dsa.doubly-ll.explain:
- A **Doubly Linked List (DLL)** is a linear data structure where each node contains three fields: `data`, a pointer to the **next** node, and a pointer to the **previous** node.
- It allows traversal in both forward and backward directions, unlike a singly linked list which can only move forward. This bidirectional navigation makes insertions and deletions at both ends (and in the middle) more efficient.
- In real life, think of a **train** where each carriage knows which carriage is in front of it and which is behind it. You can board or alight from either end without having to travel the whole train.
- DLLs are widely used in browsers (back/forward history), music playlists, and undo‑redo stacks where you need to move back and forth quickly.
how: Create a node struct with `data`, `prev`, and `next` members
Initialize `head` (and optionally `tail`) to `nullptr`
To insert at the front: set newNode->next = head; if head != nullptr set head->prev = newNode; update head
To insert at the end: traverse to tail or keep a tail pointer; adjust newNode->prev and tail->next
To delete a node: reconnect its `prev->next` to `next` and `next->prev` to `prev`; handle head/tail edge cases
Traverse forward using `curr = curr->next` or backward using `curr = curr->prev`
keyPoints: Each node stores two links (`prev` and `next`)
Insertion/deletion at both ends is O(1) if you keep a tail pointer
Memory overhead is higher than singly linked list (extra pointer)
Common operations: push_front, push_back, pop_front, pop_back, insert_at, delete_at
Useful for implementing deque, LRU cache, and navigation histories
mistakes: Forgetting to update the `prev` pointer when inserting at the front – leads to broken backward traversal; always set `newNode->next->prev = newNode` if `newNode->next` exists
Deleting the head without moving `head` to `head->next` – results in dangling pointer; update `head` and set new head's `prev` to nullptr
Assuming O(1) deletion without a pointer to the node – you still need to locate the node (O(n)) unless you have a direct reference
Memory leak: not `delete`ing removed nodes; always `delete` the node after re‑linking
dsa.doubly-ll.syntax: struct Node{int data; Node* prev; Node* next;}; // core definition
theory: What is the main advantage of a doubly linked list over a singly linked list?
It allows O(1) insertion/deletion at both ends and enables backward traversal, which singly linked lists cannot do without extra work.
How much extra memory does each node of a doubly linked list consume compared to a singly linked list?
One additional pointer (typically 8 bytes on a 64‑bit system).
Explain how you would delete a node given only a pointer to that node in a DLL.
Adjust its `prev->next` to point to `next` and `next->prev` to point to `prev`, then delete the node. Edge cases: if node is head or tail, update head/tail accordingly.
Why is a tail pointer useful in a doubly linked list?
It makes insertion at the end O(1) instead of O(n) because you can directly access the last node.
Can a doubly linked list be used to implement a stack? How?
Yes, treat the head as the top of the stack; push and pop are O(1) using `pushFront` and `popFront`.

dsa.string-hashing.explain:
String Hashing is a technique used to map strings to integer values, allowing us to compare two strings or substrings in $O(1)$ time instead of character-by-character comparison which takes $O(L)$ time.

In competitive programming and advanced data structures (like Rabin-Karp pattern matching), we typically use **Polynomial Rolling Hash**. We treat a string as a number in a large base (e.g., $31$ or $53$), modulo a large prime number (e.g., $10^9 + 7$) to prevent overflow.

Why does it matter? If you need to check if a substring of length $L$ matches a pattern thousands of times, naive comparisons will TLE (Time Limit Exceeded). Precomputing prefix hashes allows constant-time query.

Think of it like a cryptographic fingerprint or a barcode scanner at a supermarket. Instead of reading every ingredient label on a box (comparing every character), the cashier scans a barcode (hash value) to instantly identify the exact product.
how: Choose a prime base $p$ (e.g., $31$ for lowercase English letters) and a large modulo $m$ (e.g., $10^9 + 7$).
Precompute powers of the base $p^i \pmod m$ up to the maximum string length.
Compute the prefix hash array where $H[i] = (H[i-1] * p + (S[i] - 'a' + 1)) \pmod m$.
Use modular arithmetic to isolate the hash of any substring in $O(1)$ time: $subHash = (H[R] - H[L-1] * p^{R-L+1}) \pmod m$.
keyPoints: Allows $O(1)$ substring comparisons after $O(n)$ precomputation.
Polynomial rolling hash formula: $hash(S) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} S[i] \cdot p^{n-1-i} \pmod m$.
Always use double hashing or a large 64-bit prime modulo to avoid hash collisions.
Modular arithmetic requires handling negative results in C++ by adding $m$ before taking modulo.
Crucial for algorithms like Rabin-Karp string matching and longest palindrome searches.
mistakes: Forgetting to handle negative values during modulo operations in C++ -> Fix: `(val % m + m) % m`.
Using a small modulo or base like base 26 with no modulo -> Fix: causes severe integer overflow and frequent collisions.
Recalculating hash from scratch for every substring query -> Fix: use prefix hash arrays and powers for $O(1)$ extraction.
theory: What is a hash collision in string hashing?
When two completely different strings produce the exact same hash value due to modulo wrapping.
How do you mitigate hash collisions?
By using 'double hashing' (calculating two independent hashes with different primes/modulos) or using a 64-bit integer with large primes.
What is the time complexity of comparing two substrings using precomputed hashes?
$O(1)$ time complexity.
Why do we multiply by powers of base $p$?
To ensure character positions matter (e.g., 'ab' and 'ba' must have different hash values).
Can string hashing completely replace strcmp?
Practically yes for probabilistic checks, but theoretically no because of a minuscule chance of collision.

Find the longest duplicate substring in a given string.
Use binary search on length combined with string hashing and a hash set.

dsa.linked-list.explain:
A Singly Linked List is a linear data structure where elements (called nodes) are stored non-contiguously in memory. Each node contains two parts: `data` and a `next` pointer referencing the subsequent node in the sequence.

Unlike arrays, linked lists do not require pre-allocated contiguous blocks of memory. This makes insertion and deletion operations at the beginning extremely efficient at $O(1)$, because you only need to update pointer references rather than shifting elements.

Why does it matter? Real-world applications like undo functionality in text editors, browser history navigation, and symbol tables in compilers rely on dynamic pointer structures.

Think of a treasure hunt: each clue card (node) contains a location hint (data) and a scrap of paper pointing to where the next clue is hidden (`next` pointer). You cannot jump straight to clue #5 without following clues 1 through 4.
how: Define a `Node` structure or class containing a data variable and a pointer to the next node.
Maintain a `head` pointer pointing to the first node of the list (or `nullptr` if empty).
To insert at the head: create a new node, set its `next` to current `head`, then update `head` to the new node.
To traverse: start at `head` and follow `curr = curr->next` until `curr` is `nullptr`.
keyPoints: Dynamic size: can grow and shrink during runtime without reallocation overhead.
$O(1)$ insertion and deletion at the head/beginning.
$O(n)$ time complexity for random access or searching because elements are linked sequentially.
Extra memory overhead: every node requires extra storage for the `next` pointer.
Not cache-friendly: nodes are scattered across heap memory, leading to cache misses.
mistakes: Losing the head pointer -> Fix: always preserve a reference to the start of the list before traversing.
Memory leaks in languages like C++ when deleting nodes -> Fix: explicitly use `delete` to free heap memory.
Null pointer dereference errors -> Fix: always check `if (curr == nullptr)` before accessing `curr->next` or `curr->data`.
theory: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in a singly linked list?
$O(n)$ in the worst case.
Why is insertion at the beginning $O(1)$?
Because we only need to adjust two pointers (`newNode->next` and `head`), regardless of how many items are in the list.
What is a dangling pointer?
A pointer that references a memory location that has been deleted or deallocated.
Can you traverse a singly linked list backwards?
No, because nodes only store a forward `next` pointer. Doubly linked lists are required for bidirectional traversal.
What does the `head` pointer store?
The memory address of the first node in the linked list.
coding: Iterate through the list keeping track of `prev`, `curr`, and `next` pointers, reversing the `next` pointer at each step.
Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm).
Use slow and fast pointers. If they meet, a cycle exists.
Find the middle node of a linked list in one pass.
Move `slow` pointer by 1 step and `fast` pointer by 2 steps. When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle.

dsa.array-vs-ll.explain:
Choosing between an Array and a Linked List is one of the most fundamental design decisions in data structures. They represent opposing trade-offs in memory layout and operational efficiency.

Arrays store elements in **contiguous memory locations**, meaning items are packed right next to each other in RAM. Linked lists store elements as **disjoint nodes scattered across heap memory**, connected exclusively via pointers.

Why does it matter? If your application requires frequent indexing and fast lookups (like binary search on sorted data), arrays win. If your application constantly inserts and deletes items in the middle without knowing the final size in advance (like a live chat queue), linked lists win.

Think of an array as an apartment building where all apartments are lined up in a single fixed corridor with apartment numbers (contiguous). Think of a linked list as a treasure hunt where each house contains a secret map leading to an entirely different neighborhood across town (non-contiguous pointers).
how: Analyze your primary workload: Is it read-heavy (frequent random access) or write-heavy (frequent insertions/deletions)?
Check memory constraints: Can you pre-allocate a fixed-size block, or do you need dynamic resizing?
Evaluate cache performance: Arrays leverage CPU cache locality; linked lists cause cache misses due to pointer hopping.
Select Arrays if size is known and index lookups dominate; select Linked Lists if dynamic resizing and splice operations dominate.
keyPoints: Array Random Access: $O(1)$ via index math (`base_address + index * size`).
Linked List Random Access: $O(n)$ via sequential pointer traversal.
Array Insertion/Deletion: $O(n)$ because elements must be shifted.
Linked List Insertion/Deletion: $O(1)$ once the target node position is reached.
Memory Overhead: Arrays have zero pointer overhead; linked lists require extra memory per node for pointers.
mistakes: Assuming linked lists are always faster because insertions are $O(1)$ -> Fix: finding the insertion point in a linked list still takes $O(n)$ search time.
Using static arrays when the upper bound of data size is completely unknown -> Fix: use dynamic arrays (`std::vector` in C++) or linked lists.
Ignoring CPU cache effects -> Fix: arrays perform exponentially faster in loops due to hardware cache line prefetching.

dsa.circular-ll.explain:
A **Circular Linked List** is a variation of a linked list where the last node does not point to `nullptr`. Instead, its `next` pointer loops completely back around to point directly to the very first node (the `head`), forming an unbroken closed circle.

This structure is extremely useful because you can traverse the entire list starting from *any* given node and eventually loop back to where you started, without needing to know the exact position of the head. It eliminates dangling tail pointers entirely.

Think of it like a **board game with a continuous circular track** like Monopoly or musical chairs: when you reach the final property or person on the board, your next step immediately wraps you back around to GO (the beginning) instead of falling off an edge.
how: Create a standard node structure containing data and a `next` pointer.
To insert at the end, traverse until you find a node whose `next` points back to the `head`.
Update the new node's `next` pointer to point to the `head`.
Update the old last node's `next` pointer to point to the new node.
For traversal, print data and stop when your current pointer equals the starting `head` node again.
keyPoints: No `nullptr` exists at the end of a singly circular linked list; the tail points to `head`.
Allows starting traversal from any arbitrary node in the list.
Time complexity for traversal from an arbitrary node is O(n).
Finding the tail takes O(n) unless a direct `tail` pointer is maintained.
Commonly used in round-robin CPU scheduling and multimedia player playlists.
mistakes: **Infinite loops during traversal**: Using `while (curr != nullptr)` will cause an infinite loop because `nullptr` is never reached. Fix: Use a `do-while` loop or compare `curr != head` after the first step.
**Forgetting to update the tail pointer**: Leaving the old last node pointing to the head when a new node is appended. Fix: Always re-link the circular connection after insertion.
**Empty list crashes**: Attempting to insert or traverse when `head` is `nullptr` without special handling. Fix: Check if `head == nullptr` first and point the new node to itself.
theory: What is a Circular Linked List?
A linked list where the last node points back to the head node instead of nullptr.
What is the main advantage over a standard singly linked list?
You can traverse the entire list starting from any node without starting strictly at the head.
Why is a `do-while` loop preferred over a `while` loop for traversal?
Because the termination condition (`temp == head`) is true at the very start before printing anything.
How do you detect the end of the list during traversal?
By checking if the current node's `next` pointer points back to the initial starting node.
What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the end if you only have a `head` pointer?
O(n) because you must traverse the entire circle to find the node pointing to `head`.
coding: Delete a node with a given key from a circular linked list

Check if a linked list is circular

dsa.header-node.explain:
A **Header Node** (often called a sentinel or dummy node) is a special node placed at the very beginning of a linked list, right before the actual data-holding nodes. This header node does not store any valid payload data for the application; its sole purpose is to simplify structural code.

In standard linked lists, inserting or deleting an item at the absolute beginning (`head`) requires special conditional logic because the `head` pointer itself must change. With a header node, the `head` pointer *never* changes—it always points to the dummy header. Thus, every real data node has a predecessor, standardizing all insertion and deletion operations.

Think of it like a **permanent VIP parking space barrier** at the front of a lot: drivers (nodes) come and go behind it, but the barrier itself stays permanently fixed in place so the parking attendant never has to rewrite the entrance sign.
how: Initialize the linked list by allocating a dummy header node with garbage data.
Set the header's `next` pointer to `nullptr` (or back to itself if circular).
To insert at the front, insert the new node directly *after* the header node.
To delete the first actual node, update the header's `next` pointer to skip over it.
During traversal, always start your loop at `header->next` to skip the dummy node.
keyPoints: Removes edge cases for head node insertions and deletions.
The head pointer remains constant throughout the lifetime of the list.
Simplifies code readability by eliminating `if (head == nullptr)` checks for normal operations.
Consumes a negligible amount of extra memory (one extra node per list).
Frequently used in advanced data structures like B-Trees, Skip Lists, and advanced linked list libraries.
mistakes: **Accidentally printing the header data**: Forgetting to skip the header node during traversal, printing a garbage value or zero at the start. Fix: Initialize your traversal pointer to `header->next`.
**Memory leaks on destruction**: Deleting the list but forgetting to free the header node itself. Fix: Ensure your destructor explicitly frees the header node last.
**Confusing header with first data node**: Assuming `head->data` holds the first element. Fix: Realize `head` points to the dummy node, while `head->next` holds the first actual data node.
theory: What is a header node?
A dummy node at the beginning of a linked list that does not store actual user data.
What is the main benefit of using a header node?
It eliminates special-case logic when inserting or deleting at the head of the list.
Does the head pointer change when inserting elements into a list with a header node?
No, the head pointer permanently points to the dummy header node.
How do you traverse a linked list that uses a header node?
Start the traversal pointer at `header->next` instead of `header`.
What is a potential downside?
A tiny overhead of extra memory space for storing the dummy node.
coding: Implement a delete operation using a header node
Write a function that removes a node by key, leveraging the header node to avoid edge cases for deleting the first element.
Merge two sorted linked lists using header nodes
Merge two lists cleanly by attaching nodes to a single new dummy header node.

dsa.reverse-ll.explain:
Reversing a **Singly Linked List** means flipping all the directional `next` pointers so that the tail becomes the new head, the second-to-last node becomes the second node, and the original head points to `nullptr`.

Conceptually, you walk down the list maintaining three pointers at all times: `prev` (tracking the reversed portion behind you), `curr` (the node you are currently processing), and `next` (safeguarding the rest of the forward list so you don't lose it when you break the link).

Think of it like **unravelling and rewinding a line of train carriages**: you unhook each carriage one by one from the front and immediately re-hook it facing backward in the opposite direction, moving down the track until every single carriage is reversed.
how: Initialize three pointer variables: `prev = nullptr`, `curr = head`, and `next = nullptr`.
Loop while `curr != nullptr`.
Save the remaining list: `next = curr->next`.
Reverse the current pointer: `curr->next = prev`.
Shift tracking pointers forward: `prev = curr` and `curr = next`.
After the loop finishes, update your main `head` pointer to point to `prev`.
keyPoints: Time complexity is **O(n)** because every node is visited exactly once.
Space complexity is **O(1)** iterative approach, requiring only three pointer variables.
Can also be solved recursively in **O(n)** time and **O(n)** call stack space.
A classic interview coding question testing pointer manipulation fundamentals.
Crucial check: always update `head` at the end; failing to do so leaves the list detached or looping.
mistakes: **Losing the rest of the list**: Overwriting `curr->next` before saving it in a `next` pointer. Fix: Always cache `curr->next = next` *before* changing `curr->next = prev`.
**Forgetting to update head**: Reversing the pointers correctly in memory but forgetting to set `head = prev` at the end. Fix: Return or assign `prev` as the new head.
**Infinite loops with cyclic lists**: Running standard reversal on a circular linked list without breaking the circle first. Fix: Ensure standard termination conditions.
theory: What is the time complexity of reversing a singly linked list iteratively?
O(n) because each node is visited once.
What is the auxiliary space complexity of the iterative reversal method?
O(1) as only a constant number of pointer variables are used.
What does the `next` pointer do inside the reversal loop?
It temporarily caches the remaining un-reversed list so we don't lose track of it after breaking the current node's link.
What should the new `next` pointer of the original head node be after reversal?
It must be set to `nullptr` to mark the new tail of the list.
Can a linked list be reversed recursively?
Yes, by recursively reversing the sub-list starting from `head->next` and then adjusting the backward pointer.
coding: Reverse a linked list between position m and n
Locate the m-th node, reverse the sublist of length (n-m+1) using standard pointer manipulation, and reconnect the boundaries.
Reverse blocks of k nodes recursively or iteratively, checking if at least k nodes remain before reversing.

dsa.rabin-karp.explain:
The Rabin-Karp algorithm is a string-searching algorithm that uses hashing to find any one of a set of pattern strings in a text. It was created by Michael O. Rabin and Richard M. Karp in 1987. Instead of naively matching every character, it computes a hash value for the pattern and for each rolling substring of the text of the same length. If the hash values match, it performs a full character-by-character comparison to handle potential hash collisions.

It matters in campus interviews and competitive programming because it optimizes substring search from $O(N \times M)$ to $O(N + M)$ on average by using a rolling hash function (like polynomial rolling hash). This makes it extremely useful for plagiarism detection, DNA sequencing, and multiple pattern matching.

Imagine checking a long book for a specific secret phrase. Instead of reading every word character-by-character from each starting point, you assign a numerical score (a hash) to the secret phrase and to every sliding window of words of the same size. You only stop to read the words closely when their numerical scores happen to match.
how: Compute the hash value of the pattern of length $M$ and the first window of text of length $M$.
Slide the window across the text one character to the right.
Update the rolling hash in $O(1)$ time by subtracting the contribution of the outgoing character and adding the incoming character.
Compare hash values: if they match, verify character-by-character to resolve spurious hits due to collisions.
Repeat until the end of the text is reached.
keyPoints: Average time complexity: $O(N + M)$ where $N$ is text length and $M$ is pattern length.
Worst-case time complexity: $O(N \times M)$ due to frequent hash collisions (rare with a good prime modulus).
Space complexity: $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
Uses a rolling hash technique to update hash values in $O(1)$ time.
Essential for multiple pattern matching when combined with data structures like tries or sets (e.g., Rabin-Karp for multiple patterns).
mistakes: Integer overflow during hash calculation + Fix: Always use large prime numbers as a modulus and `long long` data types.
Forgetting to verify characters after a hash match + Fix: Always do a string comparison if hashes match to handle collisions.
Inefficient sliding window formula implementation + Fix: Precompute high powers of the base modulo $q$ (`h = (h * d) % q`).
dsa.rabin-karp.syntax:
long long d = 256, q = 101; // base and prime modulus
// Rolling hash update: t = (d * (t - text[i] * h) + text[i + m]) % q;
